claim: Rapid progress in technologies such as calcium imaging and electrophysiology has seen a dramatic increase in the size and extent of neural recordings.
source: Rapid progress in technologies such as calcium imaging and electrophysiology has seen a dramatic increase in the size and extent of neural recordings.
evidence: This is a general statement about technological progress in neuroscience, drawing from established scientific knowledge about recording techniques.

claim: Interpretation of neural data requires considerable knowledge about the nature of the representation and often depends on manual operations.
source: Even so, interpretation of this data requires considerable knowledge about the nature of the representation and often depends on manual operations.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges of neural data interpretation, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The deep-learning framework can decode sensory and behavioral variables directly from wide-band neural data.
source: Here, we developed a deep-learning framework able to decode sensory and behavioral variables directly from wide-band neural data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript, including decoding of position, head direction, speed, auditory stimuli, and finger movements.

claim: The network requires little user input and generalizes across stimuli, behaviors, brain regions, and recording techniques.
source: The network requires little user input and generalizes across stimuli, behaviors, brain regions, and recording techniques.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the same architecture to multiple datasets including CA1 recordings, auditory cortex recordings, calcium imaging, and ECoG data.

claim: The trained network can be analyzed to determine elements of the neural code that are informative about a given variable.
source: Once trained, it can be analyzed to determine elements of the neural code that are informative about a given variable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the influence analysis showing which frequency bands and channels are most informative for different behaviors.

claim: The approach was validated using electrophysiological and calcium-imaging data from rodent auditory cortex and hippocampus as well as human electrocorticography (ECoG) data.
source: We validated this approach using electrophysiological and calcium-imaging data from rodent auditory cortex and hippocampus as well as human electrocorticography (ECoG) data.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript for each of these recording modalities.

claim: The framework successfully decoded finger movement, auditory stimuli, and spatial behaviors from raw neural activity.
source: We show successful decoding of finger movement, auditory stimuli, and spatial behaviors – including a novel representation of head direction - from raw neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results showing decoding performance for each of these variables.

claim: A novel representation of head direction was discovered.
source: We show successful decoding of finger movement, auditory stimuli, and spatial behaviors – including a novel representation of head direction - from raw neural activity.
evidence: This refers to the discovery of head direction encoding in CA1 interneurons, which is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Orientation selectivity in V1 was identified by Hubel et al., 1959.
source: The task is complex, and although there have been notable successes – such as the identification of orientation selectivity in V1 (Hubel et al., 1959)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original work.

claim: Hippocampal place cells provide a representation of self-location.
source: and the representation of self-location provided by hippocampal place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original work and is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Neural activity is high dimensional and often sparse.
source: Neural activity is high dimensional and often sparse, while the available datasets are typically incomplete, being both temporally and spatially limited.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about neural activity patterns.

claim: The neural code is multiplexed and functionally distributed.
source: This problem is compounded by the fact that the code is multiplexed and functionally distributed (Walker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2011.

claim: Activity in a single brain region may simultaneously represent multiple variables to differing extents across different elements of the neural population.
source: As such, activity in a single region may simultaneously represent multiple variables, to differing extents, across different elements of the neural population.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural coding based on established knowledge and is illustrated with the entorhinal cortex example.

claim: Entorhinal cortex recordings contain spike trains from cells encoding head direction, self-location, and movement speed via their firing rates.
source: Taking the entorhinal cortex for example, a typical electrophysiological recording might contain spike trains from distinct cells predominantly encoding head direction, self-location, and movement speed via their firing rates (Sargolini et al., 2006; Kropff et al., 2015; Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sargolini et al., 2006; Kropff et al., 2015; Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Some entorhinal neurons have complex composite representations.
source: while other neurons have more complex composite representations (Hardcastle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hardcastle et al., 2017.

claim: Information about speed and location can be identified from the local field potential (LFP).
source: At the same time, information about speed and location can also be identified from the local field potential (LFP) (McFarland et al., 1975)
evidence: This is supported by citation to McFarland et al., 1975.

claim: Information can be identified from the relative timing of action potentials.
source: and the relative timing of action potentials (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993.

claim: Place cells have sparse firing fields that convey considerable information about an animal's self-location.
source: An experimenter, guided by existing knowledge, must recognize the fact that the activity covaries with some other factor. Necessarily this is an incremental process, favoring identification of the simplest and most robust representations, such as the sparse firing fields of place cells (Muller et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller et al., 1987 and is established knowledge.

claim: Classical methods like linear regression and linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade models provide powerful tools for characterization of existing representations but are less useful for identification of novel responses.
source: Classical methods, like linear regression and linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade models (Corrado et al., 2005; Kropff et al., 2015), provide powerful tools for the characterization of existing representations but are less useful for the identification of novel responses
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of classical methods, supported by citations and general knowledge.

claim: Classical methods typically require highly processed data in conjunction with strong assumptions about the neural response.
source: they typically require highly processed data in conjunction with strong assumptions about the neural response, and in the former cases are limited to one dimensional variables.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements and limitations of classical methods based on established knowledge.

claim: Artificial neural networks trained using error backpropagation regularly exceed human-level performance on tasks mapping high dimensional data to lower dimensional labels.
source: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) trained using error backpropagation regularly exceed human-level performance on tasks in which high dimensional data is mapped to lower dimensional labels (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Mnih et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Mnih et al., 2015.

claim: ANNs have successfully been applied to processed neural data to accurately decode behavioral variables from observed neural firing rates.
source: Indeed, these tools have successfully been applied to processed neural data – accurately decoding behavioral variables from observed neural firing rates (Glaser et al., 2017; Tampuu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glaser et al., 2017; Tampuu et al., 2018.

claim: The true advantage of ANNs is that they make few assumptions about the structure of the input data and can be analyzed to determine which elements are most informative.
source: However, the true advantage of ANNs is not their impressive accuracy but rather the fact that they make few assumptions about the structure of the input data and, once trained, can be analyzed to determine which elements of the input, or indeed combination of elements, are most informative (Cichy et al., 2019; Hasson et al., 2020; Cammarata et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cichy et al., 2019; Hasson et al., 2020; Cammarata et al., 2020.

claim: The convolutional network was designed to take minimally processed, wide-band neural data as input and predict behaviors or co-recorded stimuli.
source: To test this proposal, we developed a convolutional network (LeCun et al., 2015) able to take minimally processed, wide-band neural data as input and predict behaviors or other co-recorded stimuli.
evidence: This describes the design of the model, which is then validated through experiments.

claim: The network accurately decoded the animals' location, speed, and head direction without spike sorting or additional user input.
source: In the first instance, we trained the model with unfiltered and unclustered electrophysiological recordings made from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer in freely foraging rodents. As expected, the network accurately decoded the animals' location, speed, and head direction – without spike sorting or additional user input.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Analysis of the trained network showed that it had 'discovered' place cells.
source: Analysis of the trained network showed that it had 'discovered' place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978) – frequency bands associated with pyramidal waveforms being highly informative about self-location (Epsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis showing that frequency bands associated with place cell action potentials were most informative for position decoding.

claim: The network successfully recognized that theta-band oscillations in the LFP were informative about running speed.
source: Equally, it successfully recognized that theta-band oscillations in the LFP were informative about running speed (McFarland et al., 1975; Jeewajee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis showing that the 10.4 Hz frequency band was most influential for speed decoding.

claim: The network identified a population of putative CA1 interneurons that encoded information about head direction.
source: Unexpectedly, the network also identified a population of putative CA1 interneurons that encoded information about head direction.
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis and subsequent validation using conventional methods.

claim: The firing rate of CA1 interneurons is modulated by facing-direction, a previously unreported relationship.
source: We corroborated this observation using conventional tools, confirming that the firing rate of these neurons was modulated by facing-direction, a previously unreported relationship.
evidence: This is supported by the conventional analysis of interneuron firing rates showing directional modulation.

claim: The trained network provided a means to efficiently conduct analyses which would otherwise have been complex or time consuming.
source: Beyond this we found the trained network provided a means to efficiently conduct analyses which would otherwise have been complex or time consuming.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of frequency bands and the identification of positive interactions.

claim: Comparison of all frequency bands revealed positive interactions between frequencies associated with waveforms.
source: For example, comparison of all frequency bands revealed positive interactions between frequencies associated with waveforms – components of the neural code that convey more information together than when considered individually.
evidence: This is supported by the frequency interaction analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: The same architecture was applied to electrophysiological data from auditory cortex, two-photon calcium imaging data, and ECoG recordings in humans.
source: Subsequently, to demonstrate the generality of this approach, we applied the same architecture to electrophysiological data from auditory cortex, two-photon calcium imaging data acquired while mice explored a virtual environment as well as ECoG recordings in humans performing finger movements (Schalk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results presented for each of these datasets.

claim: The model differs markedly from conventional decoding methods which often use Bayesian estimators for hippocampal recordings in conjunction with highly processed neural data.
source: Our model differs markedly from conventional decoding methods which often use Bayesian estimators (Zhang et al., 1998) for hippocampal recordings in conjunction with highly processed neural data or linear methods for movement decoding (Antelis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison statement supported by citations to conventional methods.

claim: Conventional processing of extracellular recordings discards information in frequency bands outside of the spike range.
source: In the case of extracellular recordings, this usually implies that time-series are filtered and processed to detect action potentials and assign them to specific neurons. Necessarily this discards information in frequency bands outside of the spike range
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional processing methods based on established knowledge.

claim: Spike sorting potentially introduces biases implicit in the algorithm used and operator's subjective preferences.
source: potentially introducing biases implicit in the algorithm used (Pachitariu et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017; Hyung et al., 2017) and operator's subjective preferences (Harris et al., 2000; Wood et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers discussing biases in spike sorting.

claim: Despite considerable advances, spike sorting still demands manual input to adjust clusters.
source: and – despite considerable advances – still demands manual input to adjust clusters (Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pachitariu et al., 2016.

claim: Accurate calculation of prior expectations for Bayesian decoding requires considerable knowledge about the structure of the neural signal and appropriate noise models.
source: Furthermore, accurate calculation of prior expectations regarding the way in which the data varies with the decoded variable – an essential component of Bayesian decoding – requires considerable knowledge about the structure of the neural signal being studied and appropriate noise models.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements of Bayesian decoding based on established knowledge.

claim: Some authors have attempted decoding without assigning action potentials to specific neurons.
source: Other authors have attempted to address some of these shortcomings, for example, decoding without assigning action potentials to specific neurons (Kloosterman et al., 2014; Ackermann et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kloosterman et al., 2014; Ackermann et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2015.

claim: Some authors have combined LFP and spiking data for cursor control in patients.
source: or combining LFP and spiking data (Stavisky et al., 2015) for cursor control in patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stavisky et al., 2015.

claim: Previous approaches relied on existing assumptions about neural coding statistics and did not use all available information in the recordings.
source: However, these approaches relied on existing assumptions about neural coding statistics and did not use all available information in the recordings, while their primary focus was simply to improve decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a critical statement about previous approaches based on the cited literature.

claim: The flexible, general-purpose approach described requires few assumptions and can be interrogated to inform the discovery of novel neural representations.
source: In contrast, the flexible, general-purpose approach we describe here requires few assumptions and – once trained – can be interrogated to inform the discovery of novel neural representations.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results showing discovery of interneuron head direction encoding.

claim: The model does not rely on specific oscillations or spike waveforms and can easily generalize across domains.
source: In addition, as the model does not rely on specific oscillations or spike waveforms, it can easily generalize across domains – a fact we demonstrate with optical imaging data acquired in rodents as well as human ECoG signals.
evidence: This is supported by the successful application to multiple recording modalities.

claim: The model first transforms the neural data into frequency space via a wavelet transformation.
source: The model first transforms the neural data into frequency space via a wavelet transformation.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing step of the model.

claim: The outputs (behaviors or stimuli) are resampled to match the sample rate of the neural data.
source: Next, the outputs (behaviors or stimuli) are resampled to match the sample rate of the neural data.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step for the behavioral data.

claim: The convolutional neural network takes the transformed neural data as input and decodes each output separately.
source: Finally, the convolutional neural network takes the transformed neural data as input and decodes each output separately.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the model.

claim: Extracellular electrophysiological signals were recorded from hippocampal region CA1 in five freely moving rats.
source: To this end, we used as input extracellular electrophysiological signals recorded from hippocampal region CA1 in five freely moving rats
evidence: This describes the experimental data used.

claim: Place cells from CA1 are noted for their spatially constrained firing fields that convey considerable information about an animal's self-location.
source: place cells from this area being noted for their spatially constrained firing fields that convey considerable information about an animal's self-location (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Muller et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Muller et al., 1987 and is established knowledge.

claim: Animals were bilaterally implanted with 32 tetrodes.
source: Animals were bilaterally implanted with 32 tetrodes
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: 128 channel wide-band recordings (0 Hz to 15000 Hz sampled at 30 kHz) were made while rats foraged in a 1.25 x 1.75 m arena for approximately 40 min.
source: 128 channel wide-band (0 Hz to 15000 Hz sampled at 30 kHz) recordings were made while the rats foraged in a 1.25 x 1.75 m arena for approximately 40 min
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and data acquisition.

claim: Raw electrophysiological data were decomposed using Morlet wavelets to generate a three-dimensional representation depicting time, channels, and frequencies from 2 Hz to 15,000 Hz.
source: Raw electrophysiological data were decomposed using Morlet wavelets to generate a three-dimensional representation depicting time, channels, and frequencies from 2 Hz to 15,000 Hz (Figure 1A; Christopher and Gilbert, 1998).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing method and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The model was trained in a supervised fashion using error backpropagation with the X and Y coordinates of the animal as regression targets.
source: Using the wavelet coefficients as inputs, the model was trained in a supervised fashion using error backpropagation with the X and Y coordinates of the animal as regression targets.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Test-set performance was reported for fully cross-validated models using five splits across the whole duration of the experiment.
source: We report test-set performance for fully cross-validated models using five splits across the whole duration of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the validation procedure.

claim: The network uses 2D convolutions with shared weights applied to the three-dimensional input.
source: To reduce computational load and improve test set generalization, we use 2D-convolutions with shared weights applied to the three-dimensional input (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This describes the model architecture shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The first eight convolutional layers have weights shared across channels and the final six across time.
source: the first eight convolutional layers having weights shared across channels and the final six across time.
evidence: This describes the specific architecture of the model.

claim: Weight sharing allows the model to efficiently identify features that reoccur across time and channels while drastically reducing model complexity.
source: Implementing weight sharing in this way is desirable as the model is able to efficiently identify features that reoccur across time and channels, for example, prominent oscillations or waveforms, while also drastically reducing model complexity.
evidence: This is a statement about the benefits of weight sharing, supported by comparison to a model without weight sharing.

claim: An equivalent architecture without shared weights had 38,144,900 hyperparameters compared to 5,299,653 with shared weights, an increase of 720%.
source: For comparison, an equivalent architecture trained to decode position from 128 channels of hippocampal electrophysiological but without shared weights had 38,144,900 hyperparameters compared to 5,299,653 – an increase of 720%.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model complexity.

claim: The more complex model without weight sharing took 4.7 hr to run per epoch, as opposed to 175 s with weight sharing.
source: The more complex model took 4.7 hr to run per epoch, as opposed to 175 s
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of training time.

claim: The model without weight sharing yielded less accurate decoding.
source: and ultimately yielded less accurate decoding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model accurately decoded position from the unprocessed neural data in all rats, with a mean error less than 10% of the environment's length.
source: The model accurately decoded position from the unprocessed neural data in all rats, providing a continuous estimate of location with a mean error less than 10% of the environment's length.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results presented.

claim: The network was able to identify informative signals in the raw neural data with mean error 17.31 cm ± 4.46 cm and median error 11.40 cm ± 3.82 cm.
source: This demonstrates that, as expected, the network was able to identify informative signals in the raw neural data (Mean error 17.31 cm ± 4.46 cm; Median error 11.40 cm ± 3.82 cm; Chance level 65.03 cm ± 6.91 cm; Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: A standard Bayesian decoder without a continuity prior was applied to the spiking data from the same datasets.
source: To provide a familiar benchmark, we applied a standard Bayesian decoder without a continuity prior (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015) to the spiking data from the same datasets
evidence: This describes the baseline comparison method.

claim: Action potentials were identified, clustered, manually curated, and spike time vectors were used to decode location for the Bayesian decoder.
source: To this end, action potentials were identified, clustered, manually curated, and spike time vectors were used to decode location
evidence: This describes the preprocessing for the Bayesian decoder.

claim: Data contained in the local field potential (LFP) was discarded for the Bayesian decoder.
source: data contained in the local field potential (LFP) was discarded.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the Bayesian decoder approach.

claim: The Bayesian decoder explicitly incorporates information about the probability with which animals visit each spatial location.
source: Note that while the Bayesian decoder explicitly incorporates information about the probability with which animals visit each spatial location
evidence: This describes a feature of the Bayesian decoder based on its mathematical formulation.

claim: The CNN is effectively feed-forward, being presented with ~2 s windows of data.
source: the CNN is effectively feed-forward – being presented with ∼2 s windows of data.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the CNN.

claim: The CNN model was consistently more accurate than the Bayesian decoder, exceeding its performance in all animals.
source: Our model was consistently more accurate than the Bayesian decoder, exceeding its performance in all animals (Bayesian mean error 23.38 cm ± 4.35 cm; network error 17.31 cm ± 4.46 cm; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: T=18, p=0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison of decoding errors.

claim: The CNN's advantage over the Bayesian decoder was in part derived from the fact that it made fewer large errors.
source: The CNN's advantage over the Bayesian decoder was in part derived from the fact that it made fewer large errors (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative error distribution shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The median errors for the CNN and Bayesian decoder were more similar than the mean errors.
source: thus the median errors for the two methods were more similar (all channels; Bayesian decoder median error 13.99 cm ± 1.77 cm, network median error 11.40 cm ± 3.82 cm).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative comparison of median errors.

claim: The high accuracy and efficiency of the CNN for harder samples suggest that it utilizes additional information from sub-threshold spikes and those that were not successfully clustered and/or nonlinear information.
source: The high accuracy and efficiency of the model for these harder samples suggest that the CNN utilizes additional information from sub-threshold spikes and those that were not successfully clustered and/or nonlinear information which is not available to the Bayesian decoder.
evidence: This is an inference based on the performance comparison between the CNN and Bayesian decoder.

claim: The relative advantage of the CNN over the Bayesian decoder increased when the number of channels was downsampled.
source: The relative advantage over the Bayesian decoder increased further when the number of channels used for decoding was downsampled to simulate smaller recordings (linear regression Wald-test (n=31), s=-0.65, p=1.83e-10; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The CNN achieved similar mean decoding performance with twenty tetrodes (80 channels, 23.45 cm ± 3.15 cm) as the Bayesian decoder reached with the full data set (128 channels, 23.25 cm ± 2.79 cm).
source: Notably, the model achieved a similar mean decoding performance with twenty tetrodes (80 channels, 23.45 cm ± 3.15 cm) as the Bayesian decoder reached with the full data set (128 channels, 23.25 cm ± 2.79 cm, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative comparison shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The Bayesian decoder was only applied to periods when the animal was travelling at >3cm/s.
source: Note that for these comparisons, the Bayesian decoder was only applied to periods when the animal was travelling at >3cm/s
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the Bayesian decoder application.

claim: The CNN did not have a speed threshold and was trained on moving and stationary periods.
source: in contrast the CNN did not have a speed threshold (i.e. is trained on moving and stationary periods).
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the CNN training.

claim: Limiting the CNN to only periods of movement improves its performance, accentuating the difference between it and the Bayes decoder.
source: As expected, limiting the CNN to only periods of movement actually improves its performance, accentuating the difference between it and the Bayes decoder (0 cm/s speed threshold: Bayesian mean error 22.23 cm ± 3.72 cm; network error 17.37 cm ± 3.58 cm; 25 cm/s speed threshold: Bayesian mean error 17.17 cm ± 2.788 cm; network error 13.40 cm ± 3.59 cm, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Support vector machines (SVMs) were trained using the wavelet transformed data to compare against the CNN.
source: To compare the CNN against standard machine learning tools, we used the wavelet transformed data to train support vector machines (SVMs).
evidence: This describes a baseline comparison method.

claim: For SVMs, the spatial structure of the input is lost as the input features are transformed to a one-dimensional representation.
source: Note that in this case, the spatial structure of the input is inevitably lost as the input features are transformed to a one-dimensional representation.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the SVM approach.

claim: Both linear (53.6 cm ± 14.77 cm) and non-linear SVMs (61.2 cm ± 15.67 cm) performed considerably worse than the CNN.
source: Both linear (53.6 cm ± 14.77 cm; Figure 1E) and non-linear SVMs (61.2 cm ± 15.67 cm) performed considerably worse than the CNN.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative comparison shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The network accurately decoded location when limited to just the LFP (<250Hz) with mean error 24.24 cm ± 6.00 cm.
source: To better understand which elements of the raw neural data the network used, we retrained our model using datasets limited to just the LFP (<250Hz) and just the spiking data (>250Hz). In both cases, the network accurately decoded location (spikes-only (CNN-Spikes) mean error 17.23 cm ± 4.69 cm; LFP-only (CNN-LFP) mean error 24.24 cm ± 6.00 cm; Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The network accurately decoded location when limited to just the spiking data (>250Hz) with mean error 17.23 cm ± 4.69 cm.
source: In both cases, the network accurately decoded location (spikes-only (CNN-Spikes) mean error 17.23 cm ± 4.69 cm; LFP-only (CNN-LFP) mean error 24.24 cm ± 6.00 cm; Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The framework is able to extract information from varied electrophysiological sources.
source: indicating that this framework is able to extract information from varied electrophysiological sources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful decoding from both LFP and spiking data.

claim: The spikes-only network was considerably more accurate than the LFP-only network.
source: Consistent with the higher information content of action potentials, the spikes-only network was considerably more accurate than the LFP-only network (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, two-sided (n=25): T=0, p=1.22e-05)
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison.

claim: The LFP-only network was comparable with the spike-based Bayesian decoder.
source: although the LFP-only network was still comparable with the spike-based Bayesian decoder (Bayesian 23.38 cm ± 4.35 cm; LFP 24.24 cm ± 6.00 cm; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, two-sided (n=25): T=136, p=0.475).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison.

claim: Spatial information is predominantly contained in higher band frequencies (150-250 Hz), likely reflecting power from pyramidal cell waveforms.
source: If we retrain the model on frequency bands 0–150 Hz and 150–250 Hz, we observe that spatial information is predominantly contained in higher band frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1), likely reflecting power from pyramidal cell waveforms reaching these frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Demodulated theta is informative about the position of an animal in its environment.
source: Note that previous studies have shown that demodulated theta is informative about the position of an animal in its environment (Agarwal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2014.

claim: In previous studies, theta oscillations were converted into a complex-valued signal carrying both magnitude and phase, whereas here only the magnitude was used for decoding.
source: However, in those experiments theta oscillations were converted into a complex-valued signal, which carried both the magnitude and phase of theta – here we only used the magnitude for decoding of position.
evidence: This is a methodological comparison to previous work.

claim: The standard decoding model downsamples the wavelet frequencies to a rate of 30 Hz, potentially discarding transient non-local representations.
source: The standard decoding model downsamples the wavelet frequencies to a rate of 30 Hz, potentially discarding transient non-local representations (e.g. replay events and theta sequences).
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the standard model.

claim: A lower downsampling factor was applied to achieve a sampling rate of 500 Hz to detect short-lived events.
source: To evaluate the potential of our model to detect these short-lived events, we applied a lower downsampling factor to achieve a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes a methodological modification.

claim: The CNN decoded transient, high velocity trajectories during immobility periods with ripples that resembled replay events.
source: Examining these periods, we saw the CNN often decoded transient, high velocity trajectories that resembled those reported in studies of open field replay which are known to co-occur with ripples (see Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The decoding error for periods with ripples was larger than for matched periods when the animal was stationary but ripples were not present.
source: Consistent with this interpretation the decoding error for these periods (i.e. Euclidean distance between the animal's location and decoded location) was larger than for matched periods when the animal was stationary but ripples were not present (n=1000, p<0.001, Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B.

claim: Putative replay trajectories were longer than trajectories decoded from matched stopped periods.
source: We furthermore found these putative replay trajectories were longer than trajectories decoded from the matched stopped periods (n=1000, p=0.003, Figure 1—figure supplement 7C)
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: Putative replay trajectories were coherent, similar to trajectories decoded during movement.
source: but were coherent, similar to trajectories decoded during movement (n=1000, p=0.257, Figure 1—figure supplement 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7D.

claim: The model captures transient high-velocity trajectories occurring during sharp-wave ripples but not during other stationary periods.
source: Taken together, these analyses indicate that our model captures transient high-velocity trajectories occurring during sharp-wave ripples but not during other stationary periods
evidence: This is an inference based on the replay analysis.

claim: It is highly likely that the transient trajectories correspond to replay events.
source: it is highly likely that these correspond to replay events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the decoded trajectories.

claim: Non-local representations are accessible to this CNN framework.
source: Thus, it seems plausible that non-local representations are accessible to this CNN framework.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the replay analysis.

claim: The spatial activity of place cells is weakly modulated by head direction.
source: Thus, the spatial activity of place cells is known to be weakly modulated by head direction (Jercog et al., 2019; Yoganarasimha et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jercog et al., 2019; Yoganarasimha et al., 2006.

claim: Place cell firing rates and both the frequency and amplitude of theta are modulated by running speed.
source: while place cell firing rates and both the frequency and amplitude of theta, a 7–10 Hz LFP oscillation, are modulated by running speed (McFarland et al., 1975; Jeewajee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McFarland et al., 1975; Jeewajee et al., 2008.

claim: The architecture and hyper-parameters remained the same for simultaneous decoding of multiple factors, with just the final fully connected layer being replicated for each variable.
source: In this more complex scenario, the architecture and hyper-parameters remained the same with just the final fully connected layer of the network being replicated, one layer for each variable, with the provision of appropriate loss functions
evidence: This describes the model architecture for multi-variable decoding.

claim: All three variables (position, head direction, speed) were decoded simultaneously and accurately.
source: All three variables were decoded simultaneously and accurately (Position, 17.78 cm ± 4.96 cm; Head Direction, 0.80 rad ± 0.18 rad; Speed 4.94 cm/s ± 1.00 cm/s; Figure 2A and Figure 1—video 1)
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no meaningful decrement in performance relative to the simpler network decoding only position.
source: with no meaningful decrement in performance relative to the simpler network decoding only position (position-only model 17.31 cm ± 4.46; combined model 17.78 cm ± 4.96 cm; Wilcoxon signed-rank test two-sided (n=25): T=116, p=0.2108).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison.

claim: A Bayesian decoder trained to decode head direction achieves a performance of 0.97 rad ± 0.14 rad using spike sorted neural data, significantly worse than the CNN model.
source: Note that, a Bayesian decoder trained to decode head direction achieves a performance of 0.97 rad ± 0.14 rad using spike sorted neural data, significantly worse than our model (Wilcoxon signed-rank test two-sided (n=25): T=47, p=0.0018)
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison.

claim: The Bayesian decoder for head direction was more accurate than would be expected by chance.
source: but more accurate than would be expected by chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test two-sided (n=25): T=0, p=1.22e-5).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison.

claim: The network was able to effectively access multiplexed information embedded in minimally processed neural data.
source: Thus, the network was able to effectively access multiplexed information embedded in minimally processed neural data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful simultaneous decoding of multiple variables.

claim: A shuffling procedure was used to estimate the influence that each element of the 3D input had on the accuracy of the decoded variables.
source: To this end, in the fully trained network, we used a shuffling procedure to estimate the influence that each element of the 3D input (frequencies x channel x time) had on the accuracy of the decoded variables (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the method for influence analysis.

claim: The shuffling approach provides a rapid and computationally efficient means of assessing the contribution made by different channels, frequency bands, and time points.
source: Since this approach does not require retraining, it provides a rapid and computationally efficient means of assessing the contribution made by different channels, frequency bands, and time points.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the shuffling method.

claim: The adjacent 469 Hz and 663 Hz frequency bands were by far the most influential for position decoding.
source: Turning first to position decoding, we saw that the adjacent 469 Hz and 663 Hz frequency bands were by far the most influential (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The highly informative 469 Hz and 663 Hz bands were the dominant components of place cell action potentials.
source: We found that the highly informative 469 Hz and 663 Hz bands were the dominant components of place cell action potentials and that in general the power spectra of these spikes strongly resembled the frequency influence plot for position decoding (Spearman rank-order correlation, two-sided (n=26) ρ=0.84, p=7.63e-08; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the waveform analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Putative interneurons were characterized by higher frequency components than place cells.
source: In contrast, putative interneurons – which typically have a shorter after-hyperpolarization than place cells (English et al., 2017) – were characterized by higher frequency components (Figure 3B, Mann-Whitney rank test interneuron (n=91) vs. place cell (n=629), U=1009.5, p=2.47e-13)
evidence: This is supported by the waveform analysis and statistical comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Putative interneurons had highest power at 5304 Hz and 3750 Hz, bands that were considerably less informative about self-location.
source: with the highest power at 5304 Hz and 3750 Hz, bands that were considerably less informative about self-location (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the waveform and influence analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: 36.2% (33/91) of putative hippocampal interneurons were modulated by head direction, a previously unrecognized spatial correlate.
source: Under this more rigorous analysis, we confirmed that a sub-population (36.2%, 33/91) of putative hippocampal interneurons were modulated by head direction, a previously unrecognized spatial correlate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the conventional analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The 10.4 Hz frequency band was the most influential for speed decoding.
source: In rodents, theta frequency and power are well known to co-vary almost linearly with running speed (McFarland et al., 1975; Jeewajee et al., 2008), accordingly analysis of the network identified the 10.4 Hz frequency band as the most influential.
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis for speed decoding.

claim: The firing rate of place cells increases with speed, captured by the peak at 663 Hz in the speed influence plot.
source: Similarly, the firing rate of place cells increases with speed, an effect captured by the peak at 663 Hz.
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis for speed decoding and established knowledge.

claim: A peak at 2652 Hz indicates that interneuron firing rates are informative about speed.
source: Interestingly a clear peak is also evident at 2652 Hz, indicating that interneuron firing rates are also informative – originating either from CA1 speed cells (Góis and Tort, 2018) or from theta-locked interneurons (Huh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis and citations to relevant literature.

claim: A peak at 3.66 Hz and 5.17 Hz corresponds to type 2 theta which is present during immobility.
source: Finally, a 4th peak was evident at 3.66 Hz and 5.17 Hz, a range that corresponds to type 2 ('atropine sensitive') theta which is present during immobility (Kramis et al., 1975; Sainsbury et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis and citations to Kramis et al., 1975; Sainsbury et al., 1987.

claim: The model architecture and hyperparameters were kept the same for auditory cortex recordings, reducing only the number of down-sampling steps.
source: The model architecture and hyperparameters were kept the same, reducing only the number of down-sampling steps because of the smaller input size (64 channels vs. 128 channels for CA1 recordings – each down-sampling layer halves the number of units in the previous layer).
evidence: This describes the model adaptation for auditory cortex data.

claim: Informative frequencies for auditory decoding were concentrated around 663 Hz and 165 Hz, indicating information comes mostly from pyramidal cell activity.
source: Informative frequencies were concentrated around 663 Hz and 165 Hz, indicating that information content about tone stimuli comes mostly from pyramidal cell activity.
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis for auditory decoding.

claim: The most informative frequency bands for calcium imaging were 0.33 Hz and 0.46 Hz, mirroring the 1–2 s decay time of GCaMP6s.
source: In the frequency domain, the most informative bands were 0.33 Hz and 0.46 Hz, unsurprisingly mirroring the 1–2 s decay time of GCaMP6s (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: The relative information content of individual cells in calcium imaging was highly heterogeneous, with a small subset (18.2%) accounting for half (50%) of the influence.
source: Interestingly the relative information content of individual cells was highly heterogeneous, a small subset (18.2%) of cells accounted for half (50%) of the influence – these units being distributed across the field of view with no discernible pattern (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the influence analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The model reached an average Pearson's r of 0.517 ± 0.160 across three subjects for ECoG finger movement decoding.
source: We reach an average Pearson's r of 0.517 ± 0.160 across three subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The model outperformed the winning performance of the BCI competition which reached a performance of 0.46.
source: outperforming the winning performance of the BCI competition which reached a performance of 0.46
evidence: This is a comparison to the competition benchmark.

claim: The model can be used on a wide variety of continuous regression problems in both rodents and humans and across a wide range of recording systems.
source: These results together show that our model can be used on a wide variety of continuous regression problems in both rodents and humans and across a wide range of recording systems, including calcium imaging and electrocorticography datasets.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental results across multiple datasets.

claim: Deep-learning based frameworks constitute a valuable tool for experimental neuroscientists to provide a general overview as to whether a variable is encoded in time-series data.
source: In sum, we believe deep-learning based frameworks such as this constitute a valuable tool for experimental neuroscientists, being able to provide a general overview as to whether a variable is encoded in time-series data and also providing detailed information about the nature of that encoding – when, where, and in what frequency bands it is present.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the utility of the approach.

claim: The network might be best used as a first-pass analysis, followed by conventional approaches to determine explicitly if a variable is present.
source: Indeed, we imagine this network might be best used as a first-pass analysis, followed by conventional approaches to determine explicitly if a variable is present – much as we did for the interneuron representation of head direction.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the workflow demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: It is highly likely that the network will perform well with neural data acquired in most experimental settings, including fMRI, EEG, and MEG.
source: While we tested the network with optical and electrophysiological data in rodents, as well as ECoG data in humans, it is highly likely that it will perform well with neural data acquired in most experimental settings, including fMRI, EEG, and MEG.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the approach.
